newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG leader says confident of army loyalty.
newsitem.headline: PNG leader says confident of army loyalty.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's new leader on Saturday declared confidence in the army's loyalty, just days after rebel troops blockaded parliament and forced prime minister Sir Julius Chan to stand aside.

Caretaker Prime Minister and Defence Minister John Giheno said relations between the government and the army had been damaged by the political crisis over Chan's plan to use mercenaries to quell a secessionist rebellion.
But he believed the tensions could be resolved.
"We have every confidence in the military for them to do the right thing," Giheno, who was sworn in on Thursday, told Reuters.
"I will try to ease the situation as fast as possible to restore (good relations)."

Giheno said he would talk soon with sacked military chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, who sparked the crisis earlier this month by condemning the $36 million mercenary contract and demanding Chan's resignation.
But Giheno said he would leave acting defence force commander Colonel Jack Tuat in charge until either Chan returned to office or a new government was elected at regular national elections in June.
"I think it would be better to leave (a decision on the post)," he said.

Chan, who had already suspended the contract with British-based Sandline International and ordered an inquiry into the awarding of the contract, stepped aside pending the outcome of the probe, in the face of widespread civil and military opposition to his rule.
Although he can resume the prime ministership if the inquiry clears him before the election, most analysts believe there is not enough time before polling starts on June 14.
The decision of Chan, Finance Minister Chris Haiveta and Defence Minister Mathias Ijape, to stand aside defused the worst political crisis in the South Pacific nation's 22 years of independence.

The 10 days of turmoil, in which thousands of protesters took to the streets, climaxed on Tuesday night when rebel troops laid siege to parliament house, trapping about 100 politicians inside after they voted in support of Chan's leadership.

Giheno has described the soldiers' actions as mutiny and said they should be charged. But he said cabinet would decide, possibly next week, if the troops should be prosecuted or if they should be pardoned in line with a request by Singirok.
The cabinet will also consider the fate of a planeload of weapons and equipment diverted to Australia at Port Moresby's request.

Giheno said some of the helicopters and weapons, destined for the mercenary operation against secessionist rebels on Bougainville island, may be given to the ill-equipped police and the rest could be sold.
"It will be up to cabinet to decide," he said.
The leader of the ill-fated mercenary force, former British Colonel Tim Spicer, remains in Port Moresby, where he is due to go on trial on two illegal firearms charges next month.
Australia said on Thursday it had diverted an Antonov 124 plane carrying military supplies to an airforce base near the northern city of Darwin.

"The PNG government was concerned about the delivery of this material to PNG in the uncertain circumstances and asked Australia to receive it and store it. We have agreed to do so," a spokesman for Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said.

Australian government sources said the arsenal included two helicopter gunships, two transport helicopters, military vehicles, assault rifles, about 500 cases of ammunition and explosives, rockets and heat-seeking missiles.
Giheno on Saturday also joined moves by the central bank and the Commerce Department to reassure foreign investors wary of the climate here after the instability.
"I would urge foreign firms should not think for one moment that the stability of the government is questioned," he said.
"We have demonstrated that."

The central bank, the Bank of Papua New Guinea, and the Commerce Department said in a joint statement on Friday the business climate was recovering after the crisis, which had wiped millions of dollars off the value of listed firms with exposure to PNG.
